sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Uno vs. Un
sections.content: When counting by itself, you say "uno." But when you put it before a masculine noun, it shortens to "un": un dólar (one dollar), un café (one coffee). Before a feminine noun it becomes "una": una botella (one bottle). For now, just remember: un + thing (masculine), una + thing (feminine). Most words ending in -o are masculine, most ending in -a are feminine.

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario: Kwik Trip Register
sections.content: Next time a Spanish-speaking customer comes through your line, try saying the total in Spanish. Even if you follow it with the English amount, saying "Son cinco dólares" before "That's five dollars" shows effort and builds connection. Start with small, round numbers and work your way up. title: Numbers 20–100
outcomes: Form compound numbers like treinta y cinco (35)
Say any price between $1 and $100 in Spanish

sections.content: You've got 1–20 down. Now let's stretch to 100. The good news: once you learn the tens (20, 30, 40...), building every number in between is just snapping two pieces together with "y" (and). By the end of this lesson, every price on every shelf at Kwik Trip is something you can say in Spanish.

items: Form compound numbers like treinta y cinco (35)

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — The 20s Are Special
sections.content: Numbers 21–29 are written as one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, veinticuatro, veinticinco, veintiséis, veintisiete, veintiocho, veintinueve. Starting at 30, you use two words connected by "y" (and): treinta y uno, treinta y dos, etc. This pattern stays the same all the way to noventa y nueve (99). Just remember: 21–29 = one word, 31–99 = tens + y + ones.

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario: Pump Numbers & Totals
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, you deal with two-digit numbers constantly: pump numbers, lottery totals, gas amounts. Practice by mentally translating every price you see during your shift. See $47.00 on the register? Think "cuarenta y siete." Pump 12 lights up? Think "bomba doce." This silent mental practice is how numbers become automatic.

title: Telling Time
outcomes: Ask and answer "¿Qué hora es?" (What time is it?)
Say any time using es la / son las + number
Communicate store hours and shift times in Spanish

sections.content: "What time do you close?" — you'll hear this constantly. In this lesson you'll learn to tell time in Spanish so you can answer schedule questions, mention when your shift ends, and understand time references customers make. Spanish time uses a slightly different structure than English, but once you see the pattern it clicks fast.

items: Ask and answer "¿Qué hora es?" (What time is it?)
Say any time using es la / son las + number
Communicate store hours and shift times in Spanish

items.notes: The standard way to ask the time
"menos" = minus/less — used for minutes before the hour
"A las" = at (for times 2–12), "A la una" for 1:00

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Es la vs. Son las
sections.content: Time in Spanish treats the hour as a noun, and hours are feminine: la una, las dos, las tres. Since 1:00 is singular, you use "Es la una" (It is the one). For every other hour (2–12), you use "Son las" (They are the...): Son las dos, Son las cinco, Son las once. To add minutes, use "y" (and): Son las tres y veinte (3:20). For minutes before the next hour, you can use "menos" (minus): Son las cuatro menos diez (3:50, literally "four minus ten").

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario: Kwik Trip Hours
sections.content: Since Kwik Trip is open 24/7, your go-to answer is "Estamos abiertos las veinticuatro horas" (We're open 24 hours). But customers might also ask about specific departments: the kitchen, the car wash, etc. Practice: "La cocina cierra a las diez" (The kitchen closes at ten). For your own schedule, practice telling coworkers: "Mi turno termina a las once" (My shift ends at eleven).

title: Money & Prices
outcomes: Say dollar and cent amounts naturally in Spanish
State totals, give change, and handle price questions at the register
Understand common money phrases customers use

sections.content: This is the lesson that turns your number skills into real register power. You already know the numbers — now you'll learn exactly how to wrap them around dollars and cents, state totals, announce change, and handle the money phrases you'll actually hear from customers at Kwik Trip.

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Saying Prices with "con"
sections.content: In Spanish, prices use "con" (with) where English uses "and" or a decimal point. So $5.75 is "cinco dólares con setenta y cinco centavos." In casual speech, people shorten it: "cinco con setenta y cinco" or just "cinco setenta y cinco." For whole dollar amounts, skip the cents entirely: "Son diez dólares." For amounts under a dollar, just say the centavos: "Son cincuenta centavos" ($0.50).

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario: The Register
sections.content: Here's your Kwik Trip register cheat sheet in Spanish. Memorize these three sentences and you can handle any basic transaction: (1) "Su total es..." (Your total is...) + the price. (2) "¿Efectivo o tarjeta?" (Cash or card?). (3) "Su cambio es..." (Your change is...) + the amount. Start using these during transactions even if you finish in English. Customers appreciate it.

title: Days & Dates
outcomes: Say all seven days of the week and twelve months in Spanish
Use hoy, mañana, and ayer (today, tomorrow, yesterday)
Communicate schedules and dates for appointments and work shifts

sections.content: Schedules run your life at Kwik Trip — shift days, delivery days, when that sale starts, when a customer's prescription is ready next door. In this lesson you'll learn the days, months, and date phrases so you can talk about when things happen. Fun fact: in Spanish, days of the week and months are NOT capitalized.

items: Say all seven days of the week and twelve months in Spanish
Use hoy, mañana, and ayer (today, tomorrow, yesterday)

items.notes: Longest day name — say it slow at first
The j sounds like English h
Literally: the end of the week
Also means "morning" — context tells you which

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Saying Dates
sections.content: Spanish dates use the format: el + number + de + month. So April 15 is "el quince de abril." The first of the month uses "primero": "el primero de enero" (January 1st). All other days use regular numbers: "el dos de marzo" (March 2nd), "el veinte de julio" (July 20th). To say "on Monday" you say "el lunes." For recurring days, use "los": "los lunes" (on Mondays). Days and months are lowercase in Spanish.

Before Friday — "antes de" = before. "del" = de + el.
You still have three days — "todavía" = still.

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario: Kwik Trip Scheduling
sections.content: Knowing days and dates is huge for Kwik Trip work life. When a Spanish-speaking coworker asks about the schedule, try: "¿Trabajas el sábado?" (Do you work Saturday?). When a customer asks about a sale: "La promoción es hasta el domingo" (The sale is until Sunday). For deliveries and stock: "El pedido llega el miércoles" (The order arrives Wednesday). Even small uses like these build real rapport.

Hoy = today, mañana = tomorrow, ayer = yesterday
